title: PSYCH READING M3 — What's tech doing to your brain?
author: C·E·L Mathayom

slides.title: What's tech doing to your brain?
slides.body: Let's read and find out.

slides.title: Grammar Entry Ticket
slides.body:
Answer the 15 questions on your paper.

You have 4 minutes.
slides.notes: 4-minute timer autostarts. Students complete the entry ticket silently. Then go through the answers one section at a time.

slides.title: Entry Ticket Answers — Part A
slides.body: 1. A2. C3. C4. D5. C
slides.notes: Q1 A — modal perfect (must have stayed up). Q2 C — third conditional (had left). Q3 C — reported speech backshift (would travel). Q4 D — future perfect (will have finished). Q5 C — non-defining relative clause (which).

slides.title: Entry Ticket Answers — Part B
slides.body:
6. A7. A8. B9. D
10. B11. B12. B13. D
slides.notes: Q6 A — subject-verb agreement, indefinite pronoun (have→has). Q7 A — comma splice. Q8 B — plural uncountable noun (informations→information). Q9 D — spelling (acomodation→accommodation). Q10 B — subject-verb agreement, head noun (have→has). Q11 B — uncountable noun (equipments→equipment). Q12 B — apostrophe (its→it's). Q13 D — spelling (goverment→government).

slides.title: Entry Ticket Answers — Part C
slides.body: 14. A15. C
slides.notes: Q14 A — inversion after negative adverbial (No sooner had the bell rung). Q15 C — mixed conditional (would be playing).

slides.title: Why is this lesson important?
slides.body:
• Your phone is part of your daily life. This topic affects you.
  • The evidence comes from real research.
  • By the end, you will have your own opinion to write and share.
slides.notes: Frame the lesson value: technology touches every part of teens' lives, the evidence is real research, and the lesson ends with students forming and writing their own opinion.

slides.title: How do you use your phone?
slides.body:
How much time do you spend on it every day?

What do you do first when you wake up?

Do you ever scroll without thinking?

Opinion — Reason — Evidence
slides.notes: Open-class discussion, no right or wrong answers. Elicit freely. The yellow O-R-E label anchors the structure students will use for the final writing task.

slides.title: Choose Your Text
slides.body: Today you choose what you read.
slides.notes: Introduce the choice: three texts at three levels. Preview the excerpts, then students choose.

slides.body:
Which text will you read?

Preview each text, then choose your level.

B2

The hidden dangers of doomscrolling

Main group with the teacher.
20 copies available.

B1

Roblox: A child-friendly game with a dark side

Work together with a partner.
You mark your own answers.

C1

The truth about brain rot

Work together with a partner.
You mark your own answers.
slides.notes: Students choose their level. The main group stays on B2 (20 copies). B1 and C1 readers work in their own groups outside the main group and will self-mark with the printed answer guides.

slides.body:
B2

The hidden dangers of doomscrolling

“When you wake up and reach for your phone, what do you do first? For many people, the answer is the same: they open a news app and start scrolling. Headline after headline brings bad news, yet the hand keeps moving.”
slides.notes: A taste of the B2 text. Ask: does this sound interesting to you?

slides.body:
B1

Roblox: A child-friendly game with a dark side

“When you open Roblox, it looks like a harmless game for children. The colourful blocks, the cute characters — everything seems friendly and safe. However, new research tells a very different story.”
slides.notes: A taste of the B1 text. Ask: does this sound interesting to you?

slides.body:
C1

The truth about brain rot

“Most of us know the feeling of mindlessly scrolling through low-quality content. We call this sensation ‘brain rot.’ The term can also refer to the content itself: the absurdist, AI-generated characters and recycled memes that flood young people’s feeds.”
slides.notes: A taste of the C1 text. Ask: does this sound interesting to you?

slides.title: Let's check your word knowledge
slides.notes: Pre-teach five key words from the B2 text. Each word uses the 3-click reveal: phonemic script, then word, then context sentence.

doomscrolling
My brother spends hours doomscrolling in bed. He reads bad news until he feels tired and sad.
slides.notes: Click 1: word. Click 2: context. CCQ: When you doomscroll, do you feel happier or worse afterwards?

slides.body:

onslaught
The shop had an onslaught of customers on sale day. Too many people came at the same time.
slides.notes: Click 1: word. Click 2: context. CCQ: Is an onslaught a small amount or a huge rush of something?

slides.body:
/ˈsedəntri/
sedentary
He has a sedentary job. He sits at a desk all day and never moves much.
slides.notes: Click 1: word. Click 2: context. CCQ: If your job is sedentary, do you move around a lot or sit still?

trigger
Loud noises trigger my dog's fear. It starts shaking every time.
slides.notes: Click 1: word. Click 2: context. CCQ: If something triggers a feeling, does it cause it or stop it?

slides.title: Let's Read
slides.body:
B2 readers: stay with the class.

B1 and C1 readers: work in your groups.
slides.notes: Direct students to their groups. B2 group works with the teacher. B1/C1 groups move together and work independently.

slides.body:
Listen & Read

Listen to the B2 text.
Follow along on your worksheet.

Then answer the 10 questions.
slides.notes: Play the B2 audio once (about 4 minutes). Students follow the text on the worksheet, then answer the questions. B1 and C1 groups read their own texts silently and answer their own questions.

slides.title: Check Your Answers
slides.body:
B2: we check together.

B1 and C1: mark your own answers.
slides.notes: B2 answers are shown in the lesson. B1 and C1 students mark themselves with their answer guides.

slides.body:
B2 — Mark Your Answers

Check your own work. 60 seconds.

1. D2. A3. D4. B5. C
6. B7. A8. C9. A

B1 and C1 readers: mark your own answers with your answer guide.
slides.notes: 60-second timer autostarts. Students mark their own sheets. B1/C1 groups self-mark with the printed answer guides. Then go through each question for explanations.

slides.title: B2 Answers (1/10)
slides.body:
Question1. What does the passage suggest about the health effects of doomscrolling?
AnswerD. Mood and fulfilment tend to drop the more people scroll.
ExplanationThe research review found that people who doomscroll feel less well and less satisfied with their lives. The other options mix up different ideas, like the effect on work.
Transcript“Doomscrolling is linked to worse mental well-being and lower life satisfaction.”

slides.title: B2 Answers (2/10)
slides.body:
Question2. What does the passage suggest about the August 2024 study of 800 adults?
AnswerA. It found that constant scrolling deepens fears about life itself.
ExplanationThe study found that doomscrolling raises existential anxiety, which the passage describes as dread about the limits of our existence. The other options mix up the three studies.
Transcript“The habit raises existential anxiety — the dread or panic that surfaces when we confront the limits of our existence.”

slides.title: B2 Answers (3/10)
slides.body:
Question3. What is the main idea of paragraph 6?
AnswerD. Research keeps finding that doomscrolling harms mental health.
ExplanationParagraph 6 is about the research on doomscrolling and what it shows. The other options mention details from the paragraph, but not its central claim.
Transcript“The research picture is clear.”

slides.title: B2 Answers (4/10)
slides.body:
Question4. Why does the writer quote the doctors?
AnswerB. To explain why people feel pushed to keep scrolling.
ExplanationThe doctors' words explain the reasons behind the habit, such as stress and the urge to keep scrolling. The statistics only show that doomscrolling and poor well-being are linked.
Transcript“Stress stokes our primary urge to scroll.”

slides.title: B2 Answers (5/10)
slides.body:
Question5. In paragraph 7, what does the word “abstinence” mean?
AnswerC. Giving something up completely.
ExplanationThe passage says cutting back is not about abstinence but about decreasing reliance. That contrast shows that abstinence means giving something up completely.
Transcript“Cutting back is not about abstinence; it's about decreasing reliance.”

slides.title: B2 Answers (6/10)
slides.body:
Question6. What does the passage suggest about people who have lived through violence?
AnswerB. They often keep reading bad news even as it harms them.
ExplanationThey scroll because they want to feel safe, but the passage says the constant exposure acts as a trigger and makes their anxiety worse. So they keep reading even though it harms them.
Transcript“People who have lived through violence doomscroll out of fear; they want to feel safe, so they try to follow everything that is happening.”

slides.title: B2 Answers (7/10)
slides.body:
Question7. What does the passage suggest about the relationship between the news and the habit of doomscrolling?
AnswerA. The steady flow of distressing stories feeds the habit.
ExplanationThe media leads with bad news, and the more people scroll, the more they feel they need to. Together these ideas show that bad news keeps feeding the habit.
Transcript“The more you scroll, the more you feel you need to.”

slides.title: B2 Answers (8/10)
slides.body:
Question8. Which statement would the writer most likely agree with?
AnswerC. People can follow world events while protecting their peace of mind.
ExplanationThe writer supports the doctors' advice that people should stay informed but protect their mental health. The passage also says stopping completely is neither realistic nor necessary.
Transcript“We need to stay informed, but not at the expense of our mental health.”

slides.title: B2 Answers (9/10)
slides.body:
Question9. The chart shows how many adults took part in two recent studies of doomscrolling. According to the chart, which statement is correct?
AnswerA. The 2023 review drew on more adults than the 2024 study.
ExplanationThe chart shows two bars: the 2023 review drew on 1,200 adults, while the August 2024 study drew on 800. So the review involved more adults.
Transcript“A review published in April 2023 analysed three separate studies involving about 1,200 adults in total. An August 2024 study involved 800 adults.”

slides.title: B2 Answers (10/10) — Summary
slides.body:
Question10. In no more than 50 words, summarise the writer's advice on how to reduce doomscrolling. Give one specific strategy from the passage to support your summary.
2 pointsRestates the advice (cut back rather than stop completely; build digital and social boundaries) AND names one specific strategy from the passage.
1 pointCorrect advice but no specific strategy.
0 pointsWrong claim or no passage reference.
slides.notes: Specific strategies students may name: keep the phone away from the bed, put it in a drawer at work, switch the screen to grayscale, turn off notifications, choose local news.

slides.title: Time to Write
slides.body: All students write their own answer.
slides.notes: Everyone returns to their own work. All students write a 70-word response, whatever text they read.

slides.title: Structure Your Answer
slides.body:
OpinionI think technology changes the way I think.
ReasonOne reason is that I spend hours on my phone every day.
EvidenceFor example, the text shows how screens affect young people.

Opinion — Reason — Evidence
slides.notes: Model the structure with the example. Students use their own opinion, reason, and evidence from their own text (B2, B1, or C1).

slides.body:
Time to Write

Do you think technology is affecting your brain?

Write a 70-word response.

Opinion. Reason. Evidence from your text.
slides.notes: All students write a 70-word response. Use the O-R-E structure from the previous slide. Collect at the end of the lesson.
